questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: An `object` declaration is initialized lazily, the first time it is accessed. So `start` prints first, then `Config.name` triggers the `init` block, then the value prints. It is not created at program start.

questions.question: What happens when you compile this?
options: Compile error: objects cannot have constructors
Compiles; `Repo.name` is an empty string by default
Compiles, but throws at runtime because `name` was never passed
Compiles; the constructor runs once with a `null` argument
questions.explanation: An `object` is created by the runtime on first access, so there is nowhere to pass arguments, and declaring a constructor is a compile error. If a singleton needs configuration, use an `init` function, `lateinit` properties, or a regular class managed by DI.

questions.question: A class can declare two companion objects as long as you give them different names.
questions.explanation: A class can have at most one `companion object`. Naming it only changes how it's referenced (`Foo.Factory` instead of `Foo.Companion`). You can still nest any number of ordinary `object` declarations inside the class.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `a` and `b` are both references to the one `Counter` instance, so `a === b` is `true` and both updates land on the same `count`. Assigning an object to a `val` doesn't copy it.

questions.question: Why do many Android codebases put the extra keys and a `newIntent` helper in the target Activity's companion object, like this?
options: Building and reading the Intent live in one place, so callers can't misuse the key or type
Companion members are the only way to make an Intent survive process death
Android requires every Activity to expose a static `newIntent` method so the manifest can launch it
It makes the Activity a singleton, so only one `DetailActivity` instance can exist on the back stack
questions.explanation: The companion acts as a factory callable as `DetailActivity.newIntent(ctx, id)`, and the key can stay `private`, so the contract is defined in one place. It has nothing to do with process death or the manifest, and the Activity is not made a singleton.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: A named companion can be reached as `User.create(...)` or `User.Factory.create(...)`, and both go through the same factory. It can call the `private` constructor because it is declared inside the class, so both names come out uppercased.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Unlike Java anonymous classes, Kotlin object expressions can capture and modify local `var`s. The variable is wrapped in a shared reference, so both clicks update the same `clicks`.

questions.question: This code compiles: the companion implements `Factory<User>`, so the bare class name `User` can be passed where a `Factory<User>` is expected.
questions.explanation: A companion is a real object, and when the class name is used as a value it refers to the companion instance. So `build(User)` passes `User.Companion`, which is a `Factory<User>`. Java static methods can't do this.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: The companion is initialized once, when the enclosing class is first loaded, which happens at the first `Foo()`, after `main` printed. Its `init` runs before the first instance's `init` and never runs again.

questions.question: What is the problem with this code, and what is the usual fix?
options: The object outlives the Activity and keeps it (and its views) reachable, so it leaks; use `applicationContext`
`lateinit` can't be used inside an `object`, so it won't compile; use `by lazy` instead
It's fine: the garbage collector clears references that singletons hold once the Activity's `onDestroy` has run
The object is re-created on every rotation, so `context` is reset to an uninitialized state and the next read throws
questions.explanation: An `object` is held by a static field and lives until the process dies. After a rotation the old Activity is destroyed, but the singleton still points to it, so the GC can't collect it. `applicationContext` is safe because it already lives as long as the process.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Nothing is created until `A.value` is touched. `A`'s initializers run top to bottom: its `init` prints, then `B.value` forces `B` to initialize. Declaration order in the file doesn't matter, only first access does.

questions.question: Given this Kotlin class, which of these Java expressions compile? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: `const val` and `@JvmField` become public static fields on `Prefs`, and `@JvmStatic` also generates a static `Prefs.load()`. Without an annotation, `save()` exists only on the companion instance, so Java must call `Prefs.Companion.save()`. `@JvmField` exposes a field with no getter, so `getDEFAULT()` doesn't exist.

questions.question: Why is the convention `companion object { fun newInstance(id: Long) = ProfileFragment().apply { arguments = bundleOf("id" to id) } }` preferred over passing `id` through a Fragment constructor parameter?
options: Fragments are re-created with the no-arg constructor, losing constructor values, while `arguments` is restored
Kotlin doesn't allow classes extending `Fragment` to have primary constructors with parameters
Companion functions run on a background thread, so the Fragment is created faster and doesn't block the UI
`newInstance` makes the Fragment a singleton, so the back stack reuses one instance instead of creating copies
questions.explanation: On re-creation the `FragmentManager` builds the Fragment by reflection with an empty constructor (unless you set a custom `FragmentFactory`), so constructor arguments disappear. The `arguments` Bundle is part of the saved state and comes back. The companion factory just gives callers one typed entry point.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: An object expression creates a new instance every time it is evaluated, so two calls to `make()` return different objects. An object declaration is a single instance, so `Single === Single` is always `true`.

questions.question: A library class `User` declares an empty `companion object {}`. How can you add a function callable as `User.fromJson(json)` without editing `User`?
questions.explanation: An extension on the companion type is called on the class name, just like a companion member. `fun User.fromJson` extends instances, so it would need `someUser.fromJson(...)`. Kotlin has no `static` or `companion fun` modifiers. This only works if the class already declares a companion.

questions.question: If two threads access the `object Database` for the first time at the same moment, its `init` block runs exactly once, without any extra synchronization on your part.
questions.explanation: On the JVM an `object` is initialized in its class's static initializer, and the JVM guarantees class initialization happens once under a lock. That makes it a lazy, thread-safe singleton for free. Mutable state inside it still needs its own synchronization.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: A `const val` is a compile-time constant, inlined at the call site, so reading `Keys.A` never loads the class and the companion's `init` doesn't run. Reading the ordinary `val B` goes through the companion, which triggers initialization right before `b` prints.

questions.question: This fails with "unresolved reference 'count'". Why, and what's the smallest fix?
options: A public property of anonymous type is exposed as `Any`; make `state` private
Object expressions can't declare `var` properties; change `count` to `val`
`state` is initialized lazily, so `count` doesn't exist yet when `bump()` is compiled; add `by lazy`
Anonymous objects must implement an interface; write `object : Any()` instead
questions.explanation: When a non-private (or inline) declaration has an anonymous object type, Kotlin exposes it as the declared supertype, which here is `Any`, so `count` disappears. With `private val state`, the anonymous type is kept and `state.count` resolves. Implementing an interface explicitly would expose only that interface's members.

questions.question: Which statements about object expressions (`object : ... { }`) are true? Select all that apply.
options: One expression can extend a class (passing its constructor arguments) and implement interfaces, e.g. `object : Base(42), Listener { }`
The body can declare its own properties and `init` blocks
The body runs lazily on first member access, just like an `object` declaration
It can declare a `const val`, since it is an object
questions.explanation: Object expressions can have a superclass with constructor arguments plus any interfaces, and can contain properties and `init` blocks. Unlike object declarations, they are created eagerly at the point where the expression is evaluated. `const val` is allowed only at top level and in named or companion objects.

questions.question: `ProfileViewModel` calls `UserRepository.load()` directly, where `UserRepository` is an `object` that builds its own Retrofit API. What's the main reason this is painful to unit-test, and the usual fix?
options: It's hard-wired to a global instance, so tests can't swap in a fake and state leaks; inject an interface instead
`object` members can't be called from a ViewModel's `init` block, so the test crashes before running
Objects are re-created for every test method, so the network call happens many times; cache it in a `companion object`
JUnit can't load Kotlin objects at all without `@JvmStatic` on every member
questions.explanation: A direct reference to an `object` is a hidden, unreplaceable dependency: the test gets the real Retrofit client, and the singleton's state lives on across tests in the same JVM. Constructor injection of an interface still gives you one shared instance in the app (via the DI scope), and tests can pass a fake.
